The standard is that a Trial Chamber has an inherent discretionary power to reconsider a decision in exceptional cases if the requesting party satisfies the Trial Chamber of existence of a clear error in reasoning in the impunge decision or if particular circumstances exist justifying its reconsideration, in order to prevent an injustice. New facts or argument that arise after the issuance of the decision, may constitute circumstances justifying reconsideration. The Prosecution filed its motion on the 24th of February, 2009, requesting as its primary relief that the Chamber add the tables contained in Appendices A and B to the motion, to the Rule 65 ter list, and admit these tables into evidence. On the same day, the matter was discussed in court, and the Gotovina Defence made some provisional submissions. These can be found at transcript pages 16.732 through 16.735. Noting the absence of unambiguous objections to admission into evidence from any of the Defence teams, and the express wish of the Cermak and Markac Defence that the tables be provided to the Chamber, which it understands as an invitation to consider them, the Chamber therefore grants the primary relief of the Prosecution's motion, allowing the Prosecution to add the tables contained in Appendices A and B to its motion to the Rule 65 ter list, and admitting those into evidence. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly is invited to reconsider his nodding no. That's as far as statements of the accused is concerned. I would like to read out the Chamber's decision on Gotovina's motion to reconsider the Trial Chamber's decision of the 25th of November, 2008. On the 3rd of February, 2009, the Gotovina Defence filed a motion for reconsideration of the Trial Chamber's decision of the 25th of November, 2008, in which, forensic documents relating to the collection and burial of human remains of persons allegedly killed during and after Operation Storm were admitted into evidence. The Gotovina Defence argues that, as the Appeals Chamber granted the joint Defence appeal against the Trial Chamber's 9th of October, 2008 decision, remanding the decision back to the Trial Chamber for reconsideration, the 25th of November, 2008, decision should also be reconsidered, as it was based on the 9th October 2008 decision. On the 4th of February, 2009, the Markac and Cermak Defence joined the motion. The Prosecution responded on the 13th of February, 2009, arguing that even if the Trial Chamber chooses to exclude one or more of the 189 additional victims from the scope of the murder charges in response to the Appeals Chamber's ruling, the disputed exhibits are still relevant to issues in the trial. By way of example, the Prosecution argues that the documents are relevant to all allegations relating to notice of crimes to the accused, the pattern of killings throughout the indictment area, the widespread and/or systematic nature of the attack against the civilian population, and the accused's general failure to prevent the killings. On 16th of February, 2009, the Gotovina Defence filed a request, seeking leave to reply to the Prosecution's response, in order to cite case law showing that killing is not a crime per se; and, therefore, the evidence of killings is irrelevant to any charge in the indictment. On the 18th of February, 2009, the Trial Chamber decided to deny this request and informed the parties accordingly through an informal communication. A Trial Chamber has the inherent discretionary power to reconsider a decision in exceptional cases, if the requesting party satisfies the Trial Chamber of the existence of a clear error of reasoning in the impunge decision; or, if particular circumstances exist, justifying its reconsideration in order to prevent an injustice. New facts or argument that's rise after the issuance of the decision may constitute circumstances justifying reconsideration. The Prosecution correctly points out that in its decision, the Appeals Chamber did not exclude any of the 189 victims from the charges of murder in the indictment, but, rather, remanded the 9th October 2008 decision to the Trial Chamber for reconsideration with regard to two identified errors. All other parts of that decision remained valid. On the 2nd of March, 2009, the Trial Chamber again denied the Defence's motion to strike the Further Clarification. In this decision, the Trial Chamber granted the Defence the possibility of seeking additional time for any further investigation that may be necessary as a consequence of the decision. On this basis, the Trial Chamber finds that no clear error of reasoning or particular circumstance justifying reconsideration, in order to prevent injustice has been identified, and for these reasons, the motion is denied. And this concludes the Trial Chamber's decision on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will now deliver its oral decision on the admission of the Globus newspaper article, entitled: "Operation Storm includes an offensive on Eastern Slavonja and Baranja which was cancelled at the last minute." On the 22nd of January, 2009, during the testimony of Stig Marker Hansen, the Prosecution tendered as Globus newspaper article into evidence. The Gotovina Defence objected to the admission on the Globus newspaper article on the basis that the Prosecution had shown a lack of due diligence by not seeking to add the newspaper article to its 65 ter exhibit list at an earlier stage of the proceedings. The Gotovina Defence also objected to the addition of the newspaper article on the grounds of lack of foundation and relevance, saying that the newspaper article published in Croatia was not authored by the witness and does not reference the witness. P1291 is a Globus newspaper article entitled: "Operation Storm included an offensive on Eastern Slavonja and Baranja which was cancelled at the last minute." Part of this article has already been admitted into evidence as P701. The Chamber refers to its oral decision of the 16th of October, 2008, which can be found at transcript pages 10.758 to 10.759. In that decision, the portion of the article contained in P701 was admitted because the witness through which it was tendered was able to corroborate parts of the article with firsthand information. The Chamber notes that the part of the newspaper article that is not included in P701 and which the Prosecution now seeks to have admitted as part of Exhibit P1291 has insufficient links to the witness through which it is being tendered. The witness offers no corroboration as to the content of the newspaper article, and it is the view of the Chamber that the Prosecution should have tendered the document in its entirety at the time that P701 was tendered into evidence. The Chamber, therefore, denies the admission of P1291, and the Chamber requests the Registrar to change the status of this document in e-court accordingly. I now move to a decision in relation to Dr. Clark. The Chamber delivers its decision on the admission of the expert report of Dr. John Clark, P1251, and reasons for the Chamber's decision to consider its admission. On the 14th of November, 2008, the Prosecution submitted the expert report of Dr. John Clark, pursuant to Rue 94 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 24th of November, 2008, the Gotovina Defence filed a notice opposing the admission of the report, on the ground that the Prosecution had not notified the Defence or the Trial Chamber that it would file an expert report for John Clark. The Cermak and Markac Defence joined this objection on the 25th of November and the 4th of December, 2008, respectively. The Gotovina Defence further challenged the relevance of the expert report, arguing that John Clark was only one of six pathologists who performed the autopsies of the victims exhumed from sites in Knin. On the 12th of January, 2009, the Chamber rejected these objections and decided to consider the expert report for admission, with reasons to follow, as indicated on the transcript pages 14.127 through 14.128. On the 13th of January, 2009, after the completion of the testimony of John Clark, the Chamber invited, at transcript page 14.300, the Defence teams to indicate if there were any changes in their positions with regard to the expert report. The Defence teams did not advance further arguments on the matter. In the case of late submission of a report, under Rule 94 bis (A) of the Rules, the Chamber determines whether it would be in the interests of justice to considered admitting it into evidence. In this respect, the Chamber considers whether the report, is prima facie relevant and probative, whether the Prosecution has shown good cause to submit it at this stage, and the extent to which the submissions places additional burden on the Defence. The expert report comprises a summary analysis by John Clark of autopsy reports, prepared by six forensic pathologists, including the witness himself, of bodies exhumed in 2001 from a cemetery in Knin. The matters addressed in the expert report are relevant to the indictment, in particular, to the alleged murders charged as crime against humanity, in Counts 1 and 6, and as violations of the laws or customs of war in Count 7. For a proposed expert report to be probative, first, the author should qualify as an expert in its subject matter. The expert status of the witness, as such, was not disputed by the Defence teams. The Chamber was prima facie satisfied on the basis of the expert report that John Clark qualified as an expert in forensic pathology. The Prosecution did not put forward any argument regarding the timing of its submission of the expert report. The Chamber, therefore, found that the Prosecution had not shown good cause why it filed the expert report at such a late stage of its case, without prior notice to the Defence or the Trial Chamber. The expert report was filed on the 14th of November, 2008, and the testimony of John Clark was heard on the 12th and 13th of January, 2009, giving the Defence two months to prepare for cross-examination on matters and opinions contained in the expert report. In relation to this, the Chamber observed that the autopsy reports, death reports, post-exhumation identification, and exhumation photographs underlying the expert report appear on the Rule 65 ter list filed by the Prosecution already on the 16th of March, 2007, inter alia, under 65 ter numbers 3817, 3818, 3819, and 3820. A large number of these documents were tendered on the 5th of August and admitted into evidence on the 25 of November, 2008. In light of this, the Chamber finds that the burden on the Defence caused by the filing of the expert report does not prevent the Chamber from considering the expert report for admission into evidence. Furthermore, the expert report assists the Chamber in the interpretation of underlying forensic material, and the Chamber, therefore, found the expert report and the answers given by John Clark of high value. Balancing these considerations, the Chamber found that it would be in the interests of justice to considered admitting the expert report into evidence. The general standards of admissibility set forth in Rule 89 of the Rules applied to expert reports. Rule 89 (C) of the Rules provides this a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. In addition, the Trial Chamber's jurisprudence requires that the witness who drafted the report be considered an expert by the Chamber, and that the content of the expert report fall within the accepted expertise of the witness. An expert is a person who, by virtue of some specialised knowledge, skill, or training can assist the trier of fact to understand or determine an issue in dispute. The Chamber finds that the Prosecution has established during the testimony of John Clark his expertise in forensic pathology. It finds further that the expert report falls within the area of expertise. Having read the report, and considered the testimony of John Clark, the Chamber is also satisfied that the expert report meets the requirements for admission set out in Rule 89(C) of the Rules. The Chamber, therefore, admits the expert report of John Clark, which was marked for identification as P1251 into evidence. And this included the Chamber's reasons for considering the admission of the expert report and decision on its admission into evidence. Still a few MFIs are outstanding. We'll not deal with all of them at this moment. But the maps have meanwhile been uploaded, at least 28 of them were uploaded. The binder of maps consisted of 31 maps. One was admitted already into evidence; that was the aerial view of Knin which we've seen many times. May I ask the parties whether they agree on only seeking admission of 28 of the remaining, which means that two maps are out.

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. If I do not hear from other Defence counsel that they thoroughly disagree with you, I take it that one answer of one of the Defence teams is valid for the other Defence teams as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could inquire whether the -- Sorry, we found the mistake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a mistake but I'm happy that you found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A mistake on our side, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Mr. Registrar has meanwhile provisionally assigned exhibit numbers to the maps. The parties have received an e-mail in which they find the 65 ter numbers, and the exhibit numbers, on the assumption that the 65 ter numbers correspond with the 28 maps, the parties jointly are seeking to be admitted into evidence. The Chamber decides that P2405, up to and including P2432, are admitted into evidence. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution seeks or will seek leave to re-call the witness Rajcic. I think -- I don't know whether the application has already been filed or not. I'm not aware of the reasons, although I can guess about it. But I'll not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had intended to make oral application to the Chamber today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oral. Then please make that oral application.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. For the reasons primarily argued for the -- against the admission of the list of targets D1447, the Prosecution seeks to re-call Mr. Rajcic, Witness 175, in order to put the document to him. And determine the circumstances under which the document was created if he knows, and how that document relates to either the planning or execution of Operation Storm. Our remaining argument with respect to this, Mr. President, can be found at the transcript for Tuesday, 3rd of March. In addition to that, Mr. President, we would seek an application -- make an application for the issuance of a subpoena to Mr. Rajcic to appear for that testimony with the Court grants leave to re-call him. And finally, we would seek an instruction from the Trial Chamber to the Defence not to contact Mr. Rajcic at least until the Chamber decides with respect to our application to re-call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Is the Defence or are the Defence of the accused already in a position to respond to the oral application?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, my first question is -- is touched the last point. Have the Office of the Prosecutor contacted Mr. Rajcic already? Or did they do what they were supposed to do, go through the Victims and Witness Unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have contacted him solely for the purpose of seeing whether he is available and whether he would come without a subpoena. Nothing was discussed as to why he was being re-called or what was the purpose of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, then my next question, Mr. President, is who in the Office of the Prosecutor made that contact? Was it an investigator? Was it a lawyer? Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Does the Chamber wish us to respond to that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know yet what the relevance of the question is. Perhaps Mr. Kehoe could explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The relevance of question is, if investigators for the Office of the Prosecutor, as opposed to the Victim and Witness Unit, in fact contacted Mr. Rajcic, and we don't know what anybody talked about, how can the Prosecution stand before this Chamber and say that the Defence shouldn't talk to Mr. Rajcic when they have?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two separate issues here. There's the practical logistical aspects of, first of all, finding out if we would need a further subpoena and when that could be done and when the witness is available. And then there is a substantive issue about discussing a specific document, a specific exhibit that was not discussed with the witness initially that we want to re-call to put that document to him. So when we talk about contact, we're talking about no discussion about any substance of the testimony and we were very careful. We instructed the investigators that contacted Mr. Rajcic, and they can come and testify if Mr. Kehoe wants, and they clearly only talked about his availability, and he informed us of that, and he would not come here without a subpoena, so that we could make the oral application for a subpoena as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My initial question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, that -- Mr. Hedaraly informed you at least about what he knows or what was talked about and what instructions, explicit instructions apparently were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I would like to bring the investigator in here and have him put under oath number. Because, number one why did the Prosecutor not have the VWU and have the VWU make that inquiry as to subpoena or whatever question, and why, in fact, the Prosecution decided to use an investigator and who was that investigator? I want to cross him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- I mean, this was done clearly because of the place we are at the case now, the juncture we're at. We had to expedite matters and, I mean, these contacts are made with witnesses on a regular basis for every single witness; and frankly, Your Honour, this is just -- there just no basis, no basis for that. The basis for asking the Defence not to contact him is a very simply. Mr. Rajcic as the Court knows does not -- does not talk to the Prosecution. Last time he came here, the Prosecution had not talked to him [indiscernible] a very detailed 92 ter statement from the Defence and that's why the Prosecution wants to make sure that that document can be put in front of Mr. Rajcic without any -- any indication by the Defence as to what Mr. Rajcic may or may not say or should or should not say based on Mr. Misetic's reputation on what that specific document was. That is the basis for the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, is there any specific reason why you tend to believe that at least that's how I understood your words that -- but perhaps I'm wrong that Mr. Rajcic more was discussed than just practicalities and availability and whether he would appear without a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'll tell you the reason. The reason is the choice of who made the phone call. I didn't know who made the phone call and was just revealed that was, in fact, was an investigate as opposed to the VWU. Now normally in these circumstances, and I could be entirely wrong, but under these circumstances when we had a witness that come before this Chamber that had been in the care, custody, or control of the Victim and Witness Unit, the procedure is to contact the Victims and Witness Unit, check on this person, where he is. I don't know what other questions they ask, but I'm sure it is availability, subpoena needs et cetera, travel needs, and low and behold what do we find? We find that an investigator on that case runs back yesterday to call this guy. I trust it was yesterday because that's when we got the e-mail from Mr. Hedaraly and starts asking him questions, and we're supposed to believe that it is simply - I don't know who the investigator is - it was simply a matter of asking scheduling? Why did -- VWU generally does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Two points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. This is a repetition of your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I have to understand that the basis for wanting to hear from the investigator, whether he talked about anything else than these practicalities is because it was done through an investigator or is there any other additional reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't have any other reason other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Two quick point, if I may before that, Your Honour. If the issue is the contact had with the investigator Mr. Rajcic come. Mr. Kehoe can cross-examine on that contact so bringing the investigator now is not -- I must say in this response to my e-mail I got a response from Mr. Misetic saying now I don't think that was in jest or not that we were going to get a 92 ter statement from him this morning. I mean, I took that as being -- as being -- as being a joke about the contact. I mean, now they're being accused of contacting him, I at least have to put that on the record as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a joke, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a joke for the record. Well, that resolves at least one issue. Mr. Hedaraly, so we have two issues now. An oral application to re-call Mr. Rajcic; and an application by Mr. Kehoe for the reasons given by him to hear the testimony of the investigator who contacted Mr. Rajcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one further thing -- further clarification on the nature of this conversation. Mr. Hedaraly said they talked about need for subpoena, availability; and I'm reading from page 24, lines 20 through 25. I'd like it know what was discussed in that regard as well. I think the Chamber would as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you said and then this is an issue about discussing a specific document or exhibit that was not discussed with the witness initially that we want to re-call to -- I take it to put the document it him or to -- so when we talk about contact we're talking about no discussion about any substance of the testimony. I understood this, although the language is not unambiguous, that not in any way and in according with the instructions the investigator touched upon the substance matter of the testimony you were seeking, not even mentioning, for example, a target list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. And just to correct one last thing. There are actually three issues. There is the issue of the application to re-call Mr. Rajcic, the issue of no contact with him to discuss these matters, and also the issue of the oral application for a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I inquire whether the Defence has had any contacts with Mr. Rajcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Our -- our e-mail going back and forth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no I see that there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... well there was another one too. I gave Mr. Russo one too. There are actually two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wanted to have a clear view on all possible complications that may arise, and I want it before the Chamber will consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just want to be candid, Judge, Mr. Misetic was not the only one, and I just kind of carried it out, carried it one step further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any of the party, anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think it is on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again I want the nature of the conversation. You know, what was discussed concerning the subpoena, availability. What -- I mean there had to be some discussion as Your Honour pointed out as to why an investigator is calling a -- a -- Marko Rajic and what's the exchange back and forth, all those issues I would like to know; and I think the Chamber deserves to know, availability, subpoena, topic, all of those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hedaraly, you have been relatively shy on the matter, why you did not use the services of the victims and witness section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Frankly, Your Honour, first of all, my understanding is once the witness has -- has completed his testimony, he is no longer in the hands of the Victims and Witness Unit, and it is just a routine matter for us. Our investigators have been contacting witnesses, calling them to arrange schedules, calling them to arrange whether they would come voluntary, whether they would need a subpoena. This is -- these are things that happened throughout the trial; and frankly, Your Honour, one of the reasons why the Prosecution was able to be very efficient in bringing witnesses here and we didn't have many days without witnesses in court. And it is just the way that the Prosecution has been contacting witnesses to have them come here to testify. It was always done through the investigators on our team, and that's -- frankly the only reason that can he did it this time as well because it was the same practice and to be efficient and to get the matter in front of the Court as soon as possible, given the time -- the juncture we're at in the case right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was not the procedure that had been used with Mr. Rajcic from the get-go from what I understand. So I mean -- I don't know what he may be talking about theoretically, but if we take it back to how Mr. Rajcic was dealt with, my understanding was he had been dealt with back and forth with the Victims and Witness Unit. So I have -- I must not -- I must demere from what Mr. Hedaraly said that that was not the procedure with regard to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, when you took a statement from Mr. Rajcic, did you approach him through the victims and witness section?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you aware that the victims and witness section is offering its services to both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I understand that -- that -- we had been in discussions as you know with Mr. Rajcic prior to that time, as he told during the course of the testimony, that -- in fact, I had met Mr. Rajcic in Knin, I believe it was the summer of 2007, along with Mr. Misetic, and we were talking about various areas and discussing the artillery matters. So frankly, Your Honour, in all candor, there had been discussion back and forth, and I think Mr. Rajcic discussed those meetings that and I and Mr. Misetic and others had with him prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other, Mr. President, is -- I don't know if Your Honour wants to hear any input with regard to the merits of calling on this particular document or that's for another discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hedaraly referred to what is in the transcript, and I take it from just for efficiency reasons he explained at the time when we are discussing the admission into evidence of this -- of this target list, so there has been quite an exchange of views on the matter. Mr. Hedaraly referred to that. If you want to respond to that as well, you're free to do so. Although, of course, the position taken by the Defence not specifically in view of re-calling the witness but what the Prosecution thought that should have been done by the Defence at the time. The Chamber never decided that issue. We only decided on the admission of the document into evidence. So if you'd like to further respond to that beyond what is already on the record, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And given the oral application, it is not -- I'm not certain if we even object to the re-call of Mr. Rajcic, but I will note for the record that this particular document the Jagoda target list which is number D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are aware of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. D1447, was, of course, was not authored by Mr. Rajcic but authored by another individual by the name of Kardum, who was in the operative group -- excuse me, Operative Group Zadar at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of the details of this -- is more than aware of the details of this document and in the discussions on admissibility, I think that, Mr. Hedaraly, when explaining what he had expected the Defence to do, also pointed at the issues on which the witness could have testified, if the Defence would have done what he expected the Defence to do, so that's on the record. And in response to that - and I'm just now talking from the top of my head, Mr. Kehoe - I think that in response to that, it was argued that, first of all, that the witness was talking about targets fired at rather than just about target lists. It was our attention was drawn to the different levels of -- on which target lists were prepared; and our attention was also drawn to the fact that Mr. Rajcic, at that level, may have had no influence, may not have been aware of the existence let alone the content of those target lists. So what the party would say expect the witness could testify about or could not testify about, is to a considerable extent, I don't know whether it is complete or not, but is to a considerable extent on the record. If you would like to add anything to what you said at the time, and you're now aware of how the Chamber understands this debate on what the witness could or could not testify about, if you would like to add anything, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just taking it to one last step. If, in fact, Mr. Rajcic comes and authenticates this is document and says, Yes this is, in fact, a real document, then I would trust that the OTP is just going to accept his authenticity; absent that, if he, in fact, authenticates it, this is an exercise in futility. So if we're going to travel on this path and we don't necessarily object with if Mr. Rajcic comes in and says, This is an authenticate document, then the OTP has got to accept that. Because if they're going debate that comment then we're in a different arena, and it's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are in an area of speculation. I think, as a matter of fact, what I understood from the argument at the time was not that the Prosecution thought that the Jagoda target list should have been put to the witness just to ask him whether it is authenticate but whether he knew more about it, whether he knew more about how it was created, whether he would know more about whether it was used during Operation Storm, whether he could add anything, as he did for other target lists at a different level, whether these targets were fired at. So I did not have the impression that it was just for the authentication of this target list that you would want it recall the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, Your Honour; and we are obviously going to stipulate to anything in advance. The whole point is to have the witness come here an ask him questions on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On Your Honour's last comment, I need to inform the Chamber of a decision not made by Mr. Rajcic but made by the Gotovina Defence team. As you know Mr. Ivanovic was charged with certain crimes down in Zagreb. One of them involving this. One involving this particular document. The Gotovina Defence made a decision given the fact that Mr. Rajcic was a witness in that, not to somehow damage those proceedings by going into the details of the Jagoda list prior to that particular trial. Now that doesn't necessarily impact here, but I wanted Your Honour to have a reason why this document wasn't shown to Rajcic when we were in our 92 ter discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you will understand that the Chamber has, by far, insufficient knowledge of what could or what could not damage proceedings which are not before this Chamber, and what, if could I say, strategic or policy decisions within the Defence teams were made in this respect, and the Chamber will not further explore that as you well understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber knows what was asked, what the questions were that were put to Mr. Rajcic, and what questions were not put to him. That is for us the simple starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand that, Judge, just as a factual reason, I do believe that on concern occasions during our proceedings before this Chamber or any other Chamber that the Court deserves a reason for certain things; and that is where I was coming from. I believe that the Court deserves an explanation from the Defence as to why something happened. Doesn't necessarily go to the facts, Judge. I understand what Your Honour is saying. It is just an explanation I think the Court deserves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will consider the matter. I think that yesterday evening I seen a courtesy copy of a motion for a stay of proceedings, a joint filing by the Defence. Could the Prosecution inform the Chamber when they intend to respond and whether they intend to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, we just got it last night as well. We can try to respond either orally, hopefully. We need at least a day just to think about it and see what our position is, review the filing at this point. It's -- depending on that obviously it's going affect the response and then we can inform the Chamber as to when -- if written response is needed, how much time we would need, or if we can simply respond in an oral manner to expedite matters. We got it last night as well so we didn't have a chance to review it carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, the Chamber does not discourage you from first thinking before responding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just going back to our discussion with regard to Mr. Rajcic; and I did ask for some clarification on what exactly was discussed, subpoena, non-subpoena, availability, timing, all of those issues. Obviously we have matters that we -- I would just like the full context and full pieces of information that were told to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do encourage the Prosecution to perhaps have informal conversations which might or may not satisfy Mr. Kehoe in what he wants to know and whether he still wants the witness to be called to give further explanation about his communications with Mr. Rajcic. One very practical question: Is that investigator in The Hague; or is he any else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I believe he is -- I don't believe -- I know he is in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break. The Chamber will have to consider a few more matters. We'd like to have a longer break than usual. The Chamber would like to re-start at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber again apologises for its bad assessments of the time it needed to continue. As far as the MFI list is concerned, there is still a Prosecution's motion pending, the motion to add 66 military police documents to the 65 ter list and to admit 70 military police documents into evidence. The Chamber cannot decide at this moment because it granted Mr. Cayley another 24 minutes to file its response to that. The Chamber, however, intends to see whether we can finish at approximately 12.00 so that we immediately start, Mr. Cayley, to look at your submission, and then the Chamber has the intention to file a very brief decision on the matter, mainly informing the parties on the decision without lengthy reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have some submissions to make. They're not very controversial. First of all, it won't take long, and secondly, I think the Chamber will be able to come to a very rapid and easy decision over the matter. But -- I mean, I'm prepared to make the submissions whenever you wish me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would rather than make them orally than in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think that's probably best, Your Honour, so we can move at more speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You'd like me to do it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's do it right away. Even though it's not filed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We're talking about here about Prosecutor's Exhibit 002210 to P02312. These are not inclusive numbers. It is serial numbers 22 to 89 in the MFI list, and if I can deal with it upon the basis of the four appendices, Appendix A through to Appendix D. From the outset, I can state that we don't have an objection to any of these documents to either add them to the 65 ter list or for these documents to be admitted into evidence, but we with like to make some observations on matters of procedure, which, as with you recall, was our original area of concern. In respect of Appendix A, which concerned three documents, the Prosecution stated that the significance of these documents only became apparent during the trial, and the Cermak Defence would like to point out to the Court that, in fact, two of these documents were in the original Theunens report of December of 2007. That's P02210, which was footnote 178 in that report; and P02217, which was footnote 927 in the Theunens report. The third document, which is P02214, was footnote 3 in the Theunens addendum, which was disclosed to the Defence on the 18th of September of 2008. These are just comments, Your Honour. That's in respect to Appendix A. In respect of Appendix B, these documents were disclosed to us on the 15th of January of 2009, and that was ten days prior to Mr. Lausic giving evidence. In respect of the third appendix, which is Appendix C, and these are the 49 documents, these were disclosed to the Defence as Rule 66 or Rule 68 between 11th of October and the 14th of December, 2007, as part of a RFA package. And in respect of the last documents, Appendix D, we don't have any comments at all. So I emphasise again we don't object to admission or to these documents being placed -- the ones that were not on the 65 ter list being placed on the 65 ter list, but we make these observations for the consideration of the Chamber. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. As I said before, the Chamber intends to deliver a rather brief decision more or less of the find, as the oral decisions given in court, on this matter, preferably today; if not today, then tomorrow. Then the next item I would like to deal with is -- are the Rajcic bar table submissions. The Chamber will -- exhibit numbers have meanwhile been assigned, and the Chamber will deliver its decision. I'll try to keep it as short as possible, as far as numbers are concerned: P2433, up to and including P2437, are admitted into evidence. P2440, up to and including P2442, are admitted into evidence. P2444, up to and including P2475, are admitted into evidence. P2478, up to and including P2482, are admitted into evidence. P2484 is admitted into evidence. P2487 is admitted into evidence. P2488 is admitted into evidence. P2490 is admitted into evidence. P2493 and P2494 are admitted into evidence. P2438 and P2439 are admitted into evidence. P2485 and P2492 are admitted into evidence. Not admitted into evidence are the following: P2443; P2476; P2477; P2483; P2486; P2489; and P2491. This concludes the decision on the Rajcic bar table submissions. There is still an outstanding request, the Prosecution's motion to add one document to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. That is a motion in relation to a document which, after that, we never heard about so never any moment that it was either tendered in a bar table submission or put to a witness or sought to be tendered into evidence, and the Chamber wonders whether that motion still needs to be decided upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we would seek a decision for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it is on the 65 ter list and then to do what with it, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And then to move it into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when would you like to do that? Next year or still this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Preferably immediately after the Court's decision on the addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm lost here. My apologies. I don't know which 65 ter -- which document we're referring to, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It was the diary for TS-4, which was received by us on 13 February. We had sent it over on that date. I will have to look up the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just trying to catch up here, I mean, this was not again on a document put to Mr. Rajcic. It's part of this bar table submission? Because I don't believe that the TS-4 diary was ever shown to him. My recollection could be refreshed on that, but I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if it is not in writing there. That is the information that Mr. Russo provides to the Defence and to this Chamber. We'll further consider the matter. Then this is an decision which is, to some extent related to a decision that was, I think, delivered yesterday. That is the reasons for the decision on the Defence motions to exclude evidence of Dr. Eric Baccard and a decision on the Markac motion to exclude. On the 3rd of February, 2009, the Gotovina Defence filed a motion to exclude, pursuant to Rule 89(D) of the Rules, 44 autopsy reports admitted into evidence under the exhibit numbers P91; P728; P732; P735; P738; P1545 through P1566; P1569 through P1571; P1677; P1681 through P1687; P1689 through P1694; and two documents from the Prosecution 65 ter list with the 65 ter numbers 6053 and 6063. On the 4th of February, 2009, the Gotovina Defence filed two corrigenda to its motion. On the 4th of February, 2009, the Cermak and Markac Defence joined the Gotovina motion and the first corrigendum. The Markac Defence, in addition, requested the Chamber to exclude six additional exhibits; namely, P1544, P1567, P1568, P1573, P1678 and P1680. The Markac Defence also requested the Chamber not to admit the documents under 65 ter 6041, but since this document was admitted under Exhibit P1668 on the 12th of January, 2009, the Chamber considers this as a request to exclude that exhibit. On the 4th of February, 2009, the Chamber denied the Gotovina motion with reasons to follow, as indicated at transcript page 15.735. In the Gotovina motion, then joined by the Cermak and Markac Defence, the Defence stated that the contested autopsy reports refer to killing incidents that are not in the indictment or in the Clarification Schedule and/or did not occur in the area of responsibility of the Split Military District. With regards to some of the autopsy reports, the Defence stated that the cause and/or the date of death is unknown. The Markac Defence further supplemented these arguments by stating that the Croatian special police were not in the vicinity of the location of alleged killings at the time they occurred. Rule 89(D) of the Rules provides that the Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. The exhibits that the Gotovina and Markac sought and seek to have excluded were tendered with different witnesses and admitted by the Chamber or admitted through the Chamber's decision on the 25th of November, 2008. In the admission decision, the Chamber assessed the relevance and probative value of the exhibits mentioned. With regard to the exhibits that were admitted through the 25th of November, 2008 decision, the Chamber held, inter alia, that the autopsy reports in question relate to the death of persons during and immediately following Operation Storm and are, therefore, relevant to the indictment allegations contained in Counts 1, 6, and 7. The Chamber further recalls its Order, pursuant to Rule 73 bis (D) to reduce the indictment, the order dated the 21st of February, 2007, in which it held that the Prosecution would be permitted to present relevant evidence relating to pattern, intent, or knowledge. The Chamber considered that the Defence's arguments relates solely to the relevance and probative value of the exhibits which was considered at the time of admission. The Chamber, therefore, finds that the Defence has not substantiated its position that the probative value of the autopsy reports is substantially outweighed by a need to ensure a fair trial. As to the exclusion of the two autopsy reported from the Prosecution's 65 ter list under 65 ter numbers 06053 and 06063, these documents have not been tendered by the Prosecution. The Chamber, therefore, did not consider the Defence motion in this respect. And for the forgoing reasons, the Chamber denied the Gotovina motion in its entirety, and the Chamber also denies the Markac motion. And this concludes the Chamber's reason for the decision of the Defence motions to exclude evidence of Dr. Eric Baccard and the decision on the Markac motion to exclusion evidence of Dr. Baccard. I move on. Decisions on the fourth motion for admission of evidence, pursuant to Rules 92 quater and the Prosecution's third motion for admission of evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 bis will be filed, if not this afternoon, which is more likely the case, by tomorrow. One of the outstanding MFIs is D1083 for which a translation has not been received. The Chamber will actively seek that a translation will be delivered as soon as possible, and advises the parties - and I do see that there is a problem for the Prosecution - to seek assistance in understanding the content of it and to act on the basis, as if D1083 were admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are then still a few MFIs outstanding. We have the Lausic and some of the Rajcic MFI'd exhibits. As I said before, the Chamber will make an effort to see whether it can file - again, if not today then tomorrow - a decision in which decisions are put on paper. The Chamber is aware that, at this moment, there are certain outstanding matters. For example, no decision has been taken on whether Mr. Rajcic should be re-called or not; neither has there been a decision whether we should hear the evidence of the investigator who approached Mr. Rajcic. The Chamber does not want to rush these matters, and I give, for example, one of the reasons, Mr. Hedaraly. Let me just find it. I haven't got it here but there is some case law on whether or not once a witness has been excused and is about to be re-called what would be the proper way of dealing with that witness. The Chamber wants to give that some thought before we give a decision. But we, of course, want to take that decision as soon as possible. Mr. Hedaraly, I encouraged you to think over matters for one day. Sometimes the Chamber needs to think about matters as well. Could we receive that by when?

There is still a Prosecution's request the Chamber to order the Gotovina Defence to disclose information with regard to its communication with Croatia. We still have an outstanding request for disclosure to Croatia of concern portions of a confidential transcript. And the Chamber owes the parties still the reasons for a number of decisions. The Chamber is fully aware of these outstanding matters. At the same time, if we would wait with all of them, then we would lose time, others would say we would gain time; but at least we would move forward more slowly. The Chamber, therefore, has taken as its position at this moment that we will move on and, of course, it could well be that the still pending matters would, at any further stage, but we try to resolve most of them, giving reasons, giving a decision on the request for stay of proceedings. It goes without staying that if we would grant that motion, then, of course, the whole scheduling after the 98 bis would be quite different. We could not move on in a similar way. A decision on re-calling Mr. Rajcic might have some consequences on, as far as timing is concerned. The Chamber reminds the parties that in the interests of justice, the Chamber has the authority to change the order of -- of the presentation of evidence under Rule 85. So if there would be need to do so, the Chamber will use that authority. But, as a practical matter, and this gives a concrete answer in relation to the scheduling, as you find it in the Scheduling Order, the Chamber considers that, today, the Prosecution's case has materially been concluded. The Chamber will deliver a formal written decision next week, explaining exactly what matters are, as far as the closure of the Prosecution's case is, and the Chamber - as matters stand now, and new circumstances, of course, could change that - will hear 98 bis submissions, starting on the 19th of March, and concluding at the 25th of March. The earlier Scheduling Order counted from the conclusion of the Prosecution's case. For these mathematics, the Chamber starts counting today as the day on which, materially, the Prosecution case has been concluded, which would also mean that the Chamber sets at a date on which the 65 ter filings should be received is Thursday, the 9th of April.

Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if I could just add -- add -- add to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. And then if that would be choice of one of the defendants, then, of course, I think explained clearly then, of course, we have to face the situation we find ourselves in, and we'll seriously do that. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, and I just to put this on the record. I understand Your Honours' discretion under Rule 85, but I hasten to add the enormity of the task of investigating 189 murders. I have tried to explain in numerous, several filings the -- what we have endeavoured to do on this score; and it is something that we had fully intended to -- if Your Honour is going to consider those, take those, and take them on during the 89 bis proceeding. That's going to be virtually impossible. It was likewise virtually impossible to investigate these matters during the course of the Prosecution's cast. I think Your Honour can see that the Defence spend an enormous amount of time working on matters as they come across the transom cleaving off resources that we don't have to investigates 189 killings that came in in July of 2008 in a specific Further Clarification Schedule rendered further investigation impossible. So I -- I must put on the record and I understand Your Honours' position. It is an enormously prejudicial position for the Chamber to take for force us to move ahead prior to the 98 bis hearing without having the opportunity to fully investigate these matters. It is a matter, at this point, given the fact that it's an issue of fundamental fairness. And given the fact Your Honour -- the Chamber in its decision noted that the accused can be found guilty of murder even though the individual was not listed in a clarification schedule even though, it is not listed in a charging document such as an indictment, magnifies the importance of these 189 killings far beyond anything I think the Defence conceived of. That being the case, the -- the -- it is imperative that the -- that the Defence be able to vet these killings prior to the 98 bis motion and have additional time to do so. And they have very, very difficult to do given the scant resources or scant amount of information that comes across the transoms from the Prosecution, so I just want to put on the record the -- the tremendous prejudice to the Defence if we are forced to move ahead pursuant to Rule 85 to answer the 98 bis motion before this matter concerning 189 killings is resolved.
